dataset.name: Arctic shrub size and leaf traits, northern Alaska, summer 2017 (Version 2.0)
description: This data package contains leaf and size trait and environmental data collected from 170 plots of rapidly expanding shrub genera (Alnus, Betula, and Salix) and a widespread sedge (Eriophorum vaginatum) along a latitudinal and climate gradient in northern Alaska. The trait data were collected in summer 2017 and include leaf area, specific leaf area, leaf nitrogen concentration, leaf delta 15N, leaf delta 13C, shrub height, aboveground biomass, and the ratio of root biomass to aboveground biomass. These raw data support a submitted manuscript that examines the intraspecific variations of size, leaf and root traits of shrubs across the graminoid-dominated nutrient-poor arctic tundra and reveals the environmental drivers of deciduous shrub traits in tundra ecosystems (Fraterrigo et al., submitted). Data are presented by site (n=5) and patch (shrub or sedge plot) in separate csv files. The location data are provided in the “plot coordinates” file; all other files contain the data in the file title. Detailed methods are in the submitted manuscript. A companion data package contains root trait data collected simultaneously from the same plots (Fraterrigo and Chen, 2020). See the "Related references" section for more information.
2023/07/20 Update: The latest version of this dataset publication is version 2.0. The latest version of the data package was updated to correct the leaf size trait.csv file.

measurementTechnique:
Notes:
1. Leaf traits were measured on 10 sun-leaves collected from each target plant
2. Aboveground biomass was calculated with the allometric equations of Berner et al. (2015), using height and basal diameter measurements collected for each target shrub.
3. Organic soil horizon depth was determined for each plot by collecting an intact soil core from moss to permafrost (7.6-cm-diameter soil corer).
4. Soil temperature and soil volumetric water content (10 cm depth; Field Scout TDR 100 probe, Spectrum Technologies) were measured in three locations in each plot and the values averaged.
5. Air temperature and precipitation data for the 10-year period from 2006-2015, Climatic Research Unit (CRU TS 4.0 datasets; Harris et al. 2020).
6. Snow fall data from Littell et al. (2018), based on downscaled (771 m x 771 m) CRU TS 3.1 for the 10-year period from 2000-2009 (Harris et al. 2014).
7. AET and DEF for the 30-year period from 1975-2005 (Morrison et al. 2019).
8. Detailed methods are provided below and in: Fraterrigo, J. M., W. Chen, J. Loyal, and E. Euskirchen. Above- and belowground arctic shrub traits respond more strongly to soil factors than climate. Submitted.

Environmental measurements
To characterize regional climate, we retrieved downscaled (1 km) monthly air temperature and precipitation data for each site from the Climatic Research Unit (CRU TS 4.0 datasets; Harris et al. 2020). From these data, we calculated the following variables, averaged over the 30-year period from 1985-2015 and the 10-year period from 2006-2015: mean summer air temperature (June-August), mean winter temperature (December-February), mean annual temperature, mean summer precipitation (June-August), mean annual precipitation. Mean annual growing season length and mean annual snowfall (based on monthly snowfall equivalent data; Littell et al. 2018) at each site were calculated from downscaled (771 m x 771 m) CRU TS 3.1 for the 10-year period from 2000-2009 (Harris et al. 2014). We also retrieved actual evapotranspiration (AET) and climatic water deficit (DEF) data for each site from 60-m resolution gridded surfaces produced by Morrison et al. (2019). These water balance parameters reflect the interactive effects of energy and water on plants and are well correlated with the distribution of vegetation types across multiple spatial scales (Stephenson 1990). AET is the evaporative water loss given the prevailing water availability at a site, and DEF is the amount of evaporative demand that is not met by available water (irrespective of soil water content). Annual AET and DEF data were extracted for each site and averaged over the 30-year period from 1975-2005 (Morrison et al. 2019).
In July of 2017 and 2018, we characterized the local soil conditions in each plot. Thaw depth, soil temperature and soil volumetric water content (10 cm depth; Field Scout TDR 100 probe, Spectrum Technologies) were measured in three locations in each plot and the values averaged. In addition, we collected an intact soil core (moss to permafrost; 7.6-cm diam) from each plot to determine the thickness of the organic layer (Chen et al. 2020).

Trait measurements
In June and July of 2017, we measured leaf, size, and root traits of the target plant in each plot. We collected 10 sun-leaves from each target plant for leaf trait measurements and excavated roots in the upper 20 cm of soil. At least six intact root branches of the target shrub were excavated and carefully cut. Additionally, the basal diameter and height (H, cm) of each target shrub (ground surface to highest point of the plant) were recorded before harvesting and used to calculate aboveground biomass (Berner et al. 2015). Leaf and root samples were stored in coolers before returning to the lab, where they were kept at -20 °C until processing.
In the lab, fresh leaves were scanned to determine mean leaf area (LA, cm2) and weighed prior to drying at 55 °C for 72 h. Specific leaf area (SLA, cm2 g-1) was computed by dividing the leaf area by oven-dry mass. Roots were washed and a subsample of approximately 15 absorptive roots from each plot was selected for additional analysis. We defined the first three root orders as absorptive roots (with the first order being the most distal; sensu McCormack et al. 2015). Roots were scanned using a flatbed scanner and scans were analyzed with WinRHIZO (Regent Instruments, Quebec, Canada) to determine root diameter (RD) and total root length, which in turn was used to calculate specific root length (SRL, total root length/total root dry mass, m g-1) after oven-drying the samples. Root tissue density was calculated from RD and SRL, assuming the root has a cylindrical shape, as: root tissue density = 4 / (pi * RD2 * SRL, g cm-3). We also measured the biomass of live roots (absorptive + non-absorptive roots) in the soil cores collected from each plot (Chen et al. 2020) and calculated the ratio of total root biomass to aboveground shrub biomass to evaluate variation in allocation patterns.
Dried leaf and root samples were ground into a fine powder and then analyzed for total C and N, δ13C (leaves only), and δ15N on a Costech 4010 CHNSO Elemental Analyzer (Costech Analytical Technologies Inc., Valencia, CA, USA) interfaced with an isotope ratio mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Delta V Advantage, Fisher Scientific) at the University of Illinois. Another subset of fresh shrub root sample was preserved in 70% (v/v) ethanol for later determination of the percentage of root tips that were colonized by ectomycorrhizal fungi by inspection of root tip morphology, color, architecture, and anatomy. Additional details are available in Chen et al. (2020).
